args.text: [lane-otter] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System, the internet's address book) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to an old server that has moved or been shut down, so services appear broken. (2) Slow recovery: if a site switches to a backup server during an outage, cached answers keep sending people to the failed one. (3) Lingering bad data: a poisoned or wrong answer stays in the cache for longer, so harm from a hijack or mistake lasts longer.

[lane-otter] Idempotent retries (repeating a request that has the same effect whether it runs once or many times) matter because networks fail in ways that leave you unsure whether the first attempt worked, so you must be able to try again safely. Without this, a retry could charge a customer twice or create duplicate records, whereas with it the system can recover from faults without causing harm.

[lane-otter] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (a time-ordered universally unique identifier) as a primary key: (1) Leaked timing: the first part of each key encodes its creation time, so anyone who sees an identifier can work out roughly when the record was made, and keys can be somewhat guessable in order. (2) Size and speed cost: at 16 bytes it is larger than a plain integer key, so indexes take more space and comparisons are slower, though being time-ordered it avoids the scattered inserts of fully random UUIDs.

[lane-otter] A write-ahead log (WAL) is a record of intended changes that a database writes to durable storage before it applies those changes to its main data files. If the system crashes part-way through, it can replay the log on restart to finish or undo the work, so no confirmed change is lost and the data is not left half-written.

[lane-otter] (1) Comparable results: if the client version changes between runs, any difference in speed might come from the client rather than the thing being tested, so pinning keeps the comparison fair. (2) Repeatability: others can rerun the benchmark later and get the same setup, because newer versions may change behaviour or performance without notice.

[lane-otter] Backpressure is a signal from a busy consumer telling producers to slow down or wait when a queue is filling faster than it can be emptied. It stops the queue growing without limit, which protects memory and keeps delays predictable, at the cost of making some producers wait or have requests refused.

[lane-otter] Two ways a cron job can run twice: (1) the same job is scheduled on more than one machine, for example after scaling out or a failover; (2) a slow run is still going when the next scheduled run starts, so the two overlap. One guard: take a lock before starting, such as a lock file or a database lock with an expiry, and exit quietly if another run already holds it.

[lane-otter] A tombstone is a small marker that records that an item has been deleted, instead of removing it straight away. In a replicated store it lets every copy learn about the deletion, so a copy that missed it cannot bring the old item back. Tombstones are cleared only after a set period, once all copies have had time to see them.

[lane-otter] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) It passes and fails on the same code, so re-running it with no changes gives different results. (2) The failures depend on things outside the code, such as timing, test order, shared data or network delays, and they are hard to repeat on demand. A test that fails every time is simply broken.

[lane-otter] A lease-based lock gives a holder the lock only until an expiry time. If the holder's clock runs slow compared with the lock service's clock, it believes it still holds the lock after the lease has ended. Another process can then take the lock, so two processes act at once and the lock no longer protects the shared resource. Fencing tokens, which are numbers that rise with each grant, help the resource reject the stale holder.
